title: Living Together, Apart: A Co-housing Community in Saanich

review.notes: Solved all 9 independently; keys match. Q6 E verified (no penalty for missed kitchen duty; 'nobody keeps track' refers to diners). Distinct from other housing sets (co-housing, not laneway). No changes.

sections.label: Paragraph A
sections.text: When the twenty-two households of Garry Oak Commons moved into their new homes in Saanich last spring, most of them had already spent four years meeting in each other's living rooms. Co-housing, a model that began in Denmark in the 1970s, gives each family a private, self-contained unit but places it around shared spaces such as a large kitchen, a workshop and a guest suite. Residents design the project together before construction starts, which is one reason it takes so long. Founding member Priya Raghavan admits that several early members dropped out along the way, worn down by monthly planning meetings that sometimes ran past eleven at night.

sections.label: Paragraph B
sections.text: Money was the biggest hurdle. Because banks were unfamiliar with the model, the group struggled to secure a construction loan until a local credit union, Islandview Savings, agreed to finance the project in 2023. Each household then bought its unit outright, at prices ranging from $485,000 for a one-bedroom flat to $910,000 for a three-bedroom townhouse. Raghavan says these figures are roughly in line with similar homes nearby, so co-housing is not a shortcut to affordability. What buyers get for the money is different: the common house, with its dining room for forty people, is owned jointly, and its upkeep is covered by a monthly strata fee of about $390.

sections.label: Paragraph C
sections.text: Daily life revolves around a few shared commitments. Residents cook dinner for the whole community three evenings a week, working in rotating teams, so each adult is on kitchen duty only about once a month. Attendance is optional, and nobody keeps track of who shows up. Decisions are made by consensus rather than majority vote, a process that retired teacher Harold Beaumont calls "slow, occasionally maddening, but worth it." Last winter, for example, it took three meetings to agree on whether dogs should be allowed in the common house. The final compromise allowed them in the workshop and on the patio, but not in the dining room.

sections.label: Paragraph D
sections.text: Interest in the model is growing. Garry Oak Commons receives several enquiries a week, and its waiting list now has more than sixty names, even though units rarely come up for sale. The community runs an open house on the first Saturday of each month, and Raghavan encourages anyone curious to attend a shared dinner before making any decisions. "People imagine it's like a commune," she says. "It isn't. You can close your front door whenever you like." Two other groups, one in Nanaimo and one in Courtenay, are now at the planning stage and have asked the Saanich residents to share their experience.

questions.prompt: Buying a home in this kind of community will not necessarily save you money compared with buying elsewhere.
